result:
At 4:17 each morning, the city forgets its name.

For one minute, the street signs go blank. The buses sigh at empty stops. Apartment windows hold their rectangles of gold, but behind them nobody remembers whether they are waking or dreaming. Even the river, which has carried every reflection faithfully for a hundred years, loses track of what it is reflecting.

Mara discovered this by accident.

She was walking home with a paper bag of oranges when the world became nameless. The sign above the bakery turned white. Her phone displayed only a pale screen. A taxi rolled past with no number, no destination, no driver—just a yellow shell gliding through the blue dark.

Then the minute ended.

The signs returned. The taxi was gone. Somewhere, a child laughed in their sleep.

Mara kept the discovery to herself. She began setting an alarm for 4:16, then sitting by the window with the oranges beside her. Each morning, during that single unclaimed minute, she wrote down what she could remember: the smell of rain on hot pavement, her mother’s hands folding a towel, the exact shade of the scarf worn by a man she had loved fifteen years ago.

She wrote because she feared that the city’s forgetting was contagious.

Years passed. The notebook thickened. Her hair silvered. She moved to a smaller apartment and learned to live with the creak in her knees. Still, every morning, she waited.

Then, one day, at 4:17, the city forgot her.

Mara looked down and saw that her hands had disappeared—not vanished, exactly, but become unimportant, like details erased from a map. The room no longer knew the shape of her body. Her name fell out of the notebook. The pages continued, but the handwriting belonged to nobody.

Outside, the city held its breath.

Mara stood by the window, nameless and weightless, and watched the first birds rise.

When the minute ended, she was gone.

But in apartments all over the city, people woke with the sudden certainty that they had been loved.
